'''''Trisetum flavescens''''', the '''yellow oatgrass'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRFL5|taxon=Trisetum flavescens|access-date=15 December 2015}}</ref> or ''' golden oat grass''', is a [[species]] of grass in the family [[Poaceae]]. It is native to Europe, Asia, and North Africa.

It can be found elsewhere, such as sections of North America, where it was [[introduced species|introduced]] as a [[rangeland]] grass for [[grazing]].<ref name=grass>[http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Trisetum_flavescens&type=treatment Grass Manual Treatment] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120608015419/http://herbarium.usu.edu/webmanual/info2.asp?name=Trisetum_flavescens&type=treatment |date=2012-06-08 }}</ref> It now exists in the wild as a common [[weed]].

==Description==
''Trisetum flavescens'' is a perennial [[bunchgrass]] growing in clumps up to {{convert|60|-|80|cm|in}} tall, and known to exceed {{convert|1|m|ft}} at times.

The [[inflorescence]] is a narrow panicle which is greenish yellow to purple when new and ages to bright golden yellow.<ref name=grass/><ref>Dixon, J. M. (1995). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/2261427 ''Trisetum flavescens'' (L.) Beauv. (''T. pratense'' Pers., ''Avena flavescens'' L.)] ''Journal of Ecology'' 83:5 895–909.</ref>

The grass is susceptible to yellow oat grass mosaic virus (YOgMV), a virus of genus ''[[Tritimovirus]]''.<ref>Hassan, M., et al. (2009). Identification and characterization of a novel ''Tritimovirus'' species isolated from wild ''Trisetum flavescens'' L., family Poaceae. ''Virus Genes'' 39:1 146–52.</ref>

==Toxicity==
This grass is noted for being toxic to [[livestock]], causing [[calcinosis]], the deposition of calcium in soft tissues including muscle and [[tendon]]s, the heart and large [[artery|arteries]] including the [[aorta]]. [[Cattle]] suffer difficulty in moving and standing and reduced milk production.<ref>Braun, U., et al. (2000). Enzootic calcinosis in 16 cows from 6 dairy farms in Unterengadin. ''Schweiz Arch Tierheilkd.'' 142:6 333–8.</ref> [[Goat]]s suffer [[heart murmur]]s and [[Heart arrhythmia|arrhythmia]]s, weight loss, difficulty in walking, kneeling, and rising, and reduced milk production.<ref>Braun, U., et al. (2000). [http://veterinaryrecord.bmj.com/content/146/6/161.extract Enzootic calcinosis in goats caused by golden oat grass (''Trisetum flavescens'').] ''Veterinary Record'' 146 161–2. {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708074507/http://veterinaryrecord.bmj.com/content/146/6/161.extract |date=2011-07-08 }}</ref> [[Horse]]s suffer tenderness in tendons and [[ligament]]s, weight loss, and problems with movement.<ref>Grabner, A., et al. (1985). Enzootic calcinosis in the horse. ''Tierarztl Prax Suppl.'' 1 84–93.</ref>
